IT Cybersecurity and OT Cybersecurity personnel may be able to observe anomalous network traffic to and from C2 servers, as well as anomalous network traffic between the IT and OT environments. 
A total of five observables were identified with the use of the Lateral Tool Transfer technique (T0867). This technique is important for investigation because the adversary is attempting to move OT-specific offensive tools into the victim’s environment. This technique appears  in the middle of the timeline and responding to it may halt disruption or damage to OT assets. Terminating the chain of techniques at this point would limit additional malicious adversary activity in the OT environment as well as future disruption or damage to OT equipment. 
Of the five observables associated with this technique, two are assessed to be highly perceivable.

Multiple modules within INCONTROLLER are capable of the Theft of Operational Information technique (T0882). TAGRUN can identify a victim’s OT architecture by using OPC UA to map out OPC clients and servers throughout an OT environment. OMSHELL can capture and record network traffic related to Omron PLCs, parse network traffic for specific attributes such as MAC addresses, and export this to an adversary. CODECALL is also able to download configuration files from Schneider Electric PLCs as well as those that use CODESYS, likely to assist an adversary in developing customized payloads. 
IT Cybersecurity, OT Staff, and OT Cybersecurity personnel are not likely to observe the precursor reconnaissance activity as anomalous files present on hosts that would be sent off to an adversary. However, an adversary is likely to delete any files related to malicious scanning or network traffic captures which may present an observable opportunity for defenders
A total of 53 observables were identified with the use of the Theft of Operational Information technique (T0882). This technique is important for investigation because the exfiltration of operational information is almost certain to bolster payload development by an adversary. This technique appears in the middle of the timeline and responding to it will limit how much an adversary can learn about a victim’s OT environment. Terminating the chain of techniques at this point may halt some future events, however an adversary would likely continue to have access as well as the necessary information to develop customized payloads. 
Of the 53 observables associated with this technique, seven are assessed to be highly perceivable.

Numerous modules within the INCONTROLLER framework use the Commonly Used Port technique (T0885) to support C2 activities with an adversary. CyOTE analysts assess that ICECORE may be like other Windows malware and likely uses Ports 80 and 443 for C2 traffic, as well as Port 135 for WMI discovery activities. TAGRUN likely uses Port 7 for its ICMP Ping discovery capability, as well as TCP Port 4840 to scan for OPC UA servers, but this port can easily be changed by an adversary.  As a part of the proprietary FINS protocol, OMSHELL may use Port 23 for Telnet and Port 80 for FINS, which is based on HTTP. OMSHELL may also use Port 9600 over both TCP and UDP.  CODECALL will initially send out UDP broadcasts over Port 27127 in the OT environment; however, since this is the standard scanning port, observers should use discretion when analyzing anomalous scanning on 27127.  CODECALL can also scan for Schneider Electric devices over UDP on Port 1740-1743, TCP Port 1105, and TCP Port 11740.  CODECALL also scans for Modbus devices on Port 502.  
IT Cybersecurity, OT Staff, and OT Cybersecurity personnel may be able to observe anomalous network traffic over the aforementioned network ports. 
A total of 52 observables were identified with the use of the Commonly Used Port technique (T0885). This technique is important for investigation as it presents an opportunity for defenders to identify an adversary’s command and control traffic. This technique appears throughout the timeline and responding to it may halt future malicious activity. Terminating the chain of techniques at this point would limit adversary activity and potentially halt some future events.
Of the 52 observables associated with this technique, six are assessed to be highly perceivable.

Adversaries using the INCONTROLLER framework may use the Remote Services technique for initial access to a victim’s OT environment. OMSHELL is capable of the Remote Services technique via the Telnet protocol to gain remote access to vulnerable Omron assets.  However, it is unclear whether an adversary would require prior access to that environment or if they would be able to brute force weak credentials to internet-exposed assets to gain access. 
IT Cybersecurity and OT Cybersecurity personnel may be able to observe anomalous Telnet traffic over TCP Port 23 in their environments due to OMSHELL’s capability to access Omron assets from either a remote server or an infected IT environment.
A total of 10 observables were identified with the use of the Remote Services technique (T0886). This technique is important for investigation because improperly configured OT networks can grant an adversary access without them having to compromise and pivot from an organization’s IT environment. This technique appears early in the timeline and responding to it will likely limit the avenues an adversary can use to gain access into the OT environment. Terminating the chain of techniques at this point would halt future events by an adversary employing OMSHELL.  
Of the 10 observables associated with this technique, one is assessed to be highly perceivable.

The OMSHELL module within the INCONTROLLER framework can abuse remote services to facilitate lateral movement.  OMSHELL uses the telnet and FINS protocols to gain remote access to vulnerable OT assets such as HMIs and engineering workstations. 
IT Cybersecurity and OT Cybersecurity personnel may be able to observe anomalous telnet or FINS traffic in their environments due OMSHELL’s capability to access OT assets from either a remote server or an infected IT environment.
A total of 13 observables were identified with the use of the Remote Services technique (T0886). This technique is important for investigation because an adversary is attempting to move through a victim’s environment to conduct additional malicious activity. This technique may appear throughout the timeline and responding to it would limit an adversary’s options for access into the victim’s environment. Terminating the chain of techniques at this point may halt future events. 
Of the 13 observables associated with this technique, two are assessed to be highly perceivable.

Several modules within the INCONTROLLER malware framework are capable of the Remote System Information Discovery technique (T0888). ICECORE’s WMI scanning can likely enumerate detailed information about hosts within the enterprise environment.  TAGRUN’s OPC UA scanning also can query specific information about OPC configured assets to bolster adversary reconnaissance. OMSHELL primarily uses HTTP GET and POST requests to interact with Omron devices previously identified by FINS over UDP requests. CISA also notes that OMSHELL can parse HTTP traffic from OMRON devices to gain further insight into the victim’s environment. CODECALL will send Modbus and CODESYS traffic to identify any networked assets that respond to the Modbus and CODESYS requests, demonstrating that CODECALL not only affects Schneider Electric devices, but those that use Modbus or CODESYS. 
IT Cybersecurity, OT Staff, and OT Cybersecurity personnel may be able to observe anomalous network traffic linked to various remote system information discovery activity as well as the presence of anomalous files related to adversary activity. 
A total of 35 observables were identified with the use of the Remote System Information Discovery technique (T0888). This technique is important for investigation because it allows an adversary to gain detailed information of critical OT assets.  This technique appears throughout the timeline and responding to it may limit the amount of detail an adversary can learn about assets in a victim’s environment. Terminating the chain of techniques at this point would limit the insight an adversary can gain into specific assets within an environment. 
Of the 35 observables associated with this technique, one is assessed to be highly perceivable.

The adversary behind the creation of the INCONTROLLER framework would likely use Exploitation for Privilege Escalation technique within the victim’s environment by leveraging CVE-2020-15368, a vulnerability in an ASRock driver, allowing kernel-level execution of malicious code on an infected host.  
IT Cybersecurity and OT Cybersecurity personnel are not likely to observe the adversary leveraging this kernel-level vulnerability in an environment. 
A total of four observables were identified with the use of the Exploitation for Privilege Escalation technique (T0890). This technique is important for investigation because it results in the adversary gaining root level access to crucial systems and assets in either the IT or OT environment. This technique appears somewhat early in the timeline, and responding to it will delay adversary privilege escalation. Terminating the chain of techniques at this point would limit an adversary’s ability to conduct further malicious activity requiring higher privileges on a device or network. 
Of the four observables associated with this technique, none are assessed to be highly perceivable.

An adversary deploying the INCONTROLLER malware framework may use the Modify Program technique to bolster persistence in a victim’s environment. The OMSHELL module’s functionality would allow it to modify Omron devices to allow an adversary to upload a file to remotely connect and issue commands via HTTP traffic. CODECALL is also able to remove, modify, and replace logic on targeted Schneider Electric devices. 
OT Staff and OT Cybersecurity personnel may be able to observe anomalous HTTP or FINS network traffic related to modifying Omron PLCs. 
A total of 33 observables were identified with the use of the Modify Program technique (T0889). This technique is important for investigation because an adversary is actively attempting to maintain remote access within the victim’s OT environment to facilitate additional malicious activity. This technique appears somewhat early in the timeline and responding to it will prevent an adversary from maintaining continued access to the OT environment.  Terminating the chain of techniques at this point would limit adversary access to OT assets. 
Of the 33 observables associated with this technique, one is assessed to be highly perceivable.

CODECALL is capable of the Device Shutdown or Restart technique (T0816). CODECALL can crash CODESYS devices and conduct a “packet of death” attack which may result in the device needing to be restarted. , 
OT Staff and OT Cybersecurity personnel likely would not be able to observe anomalous reboots or malicious Modbus and CODESYS packets in time to prevent operational disruption. 
A total of 10 observables were identified with the use of the Device Shutdown or Restart technique (T0816). This technique is important for investigation because an adversary is attempting to interfere with normal processes in the OT environment. This technique appears late in the timeline and responding to it is not likely to halt future events. Terminating the chain of techniques at this point in the timeline is not likely to prevent disruption or destruction. 
Of the 10 observables associated with this technique, three are assessed to be highly perceivable.

The CODECALL module within the INCONTROLLER framework is capable of the Denial of Service technique. CODECALL can carry out a Distributed Denial of Service (DDoS) attack by disabling CODESYS connections to targeted PLCs and sending custom packets to crash any targeted PLCs.  OMSHELL can also conduct DDoS attacks to terminate any active connections to Omron PLCs.
OT Staff and OT Cybersecurity personnel may be able to observe either anomalous network connection errors or network connection failures. 
A total of 11 observables were identified with the use of the Denial of Service technique (T0814). This technique is important for investigation because an adversary is attempting to disrupt a properly functioning device, which may result in operational disruption or, in some cases, physical damage. This technique appears late in the timeline and responding to it likely will not halt all future events. Terminating the chain of techniques at this point may limit some operational disruption. 
Of the 11 observables associated with this technique, two are assessed to be highly perceivable.

The CODECALL module within the INC ONTROLLER framework is capable of the Denial of View technique (T0815). CODECALL can crash PLCs several different ways, and communications between engineering workstations and the crashed PLCs may cause a temporary denial of view scenario. A power cycle and configuration recovery are necessary to restore monitoring and communication to any affected PLCs.  
OT Staff and OT Cybersecurity personnel may be able to observe anomalous instances where OT systems are unresponsive to communications. 
A total of 11 observables were identified with the use of the Denial of View technique (T0815). This technique is important for investigation because operators and safety systems lose visibility into OT assets responsible for physical processes. This technique appears late in the timeline and responding to it may hasten operators regaining view and control of OT assets. Terminating the chain of techniques at this point is not likely to prevent operational disruption but may prevent physical damage. 
Of the 11 observables associated with this technique, two are assessed to be highly perceivable.

If deployed in a comprehensive manner, INCONTROLLER is capable of the Loss of Productivity and Revenue technique (T0828). Several of INCONTROLLER’s modules can cause either operational disruption or physical destruction, leading to unplanned downtime.  
IT Staff, IT Cybersecurity, OT Staff, OT Cybersecurity, Engineering, Support Staff, and Management personnel may be able to observe operational disruption or physical destruction that would impact productivity and revenue flow. 
A total of two observables were identified with the use of the Loss of Productivity and Revenue technique (T0828). This technique is important for investigation because it involves potential damage to not only systems, but business losses as well. This technique appears at the end of the attack and responding to it will not have any preventative effect. Terminating the chain of techniques at this point would not have any effect.  
Of the two observables associated with this technique, both are assessed to be highly perceivable.

The CODECALL module within the INCONTROLLER framework is capable of the Loss of Availability technique (T0826). Due to CODECALL’s ability to sever communications and cause a temporary denial of view scenario, this could simultaneously result in a loss of availability until remedial and recovery efforts are taken. 
OT Staff and OT Cybersecurity personnel may be able to observe unresponsive OT systems as well as anomalous behavior in physical processes. 
A total of 11 observables were identified with the use of the Loss of Availability technique (T0826). This technique is important for investigation because an adversary is attempting to disrupt OT systems or, in some cases, physical damage.  This technique appears late in the timeline and responding to it would not have any effect. Terminating the chain of techniques at this point is not likely to limit operational disruption or physical damage. 
Of the 11 observables associated with this technique, two are assessed to be highly perceivable.

An adversary employing the INCONTROLLER framework almost certainly would use the Command-Line Execution technique (T0807) to execute various tools contained within the framework. TAGRUN that targets OPC UA clients and servers, OMSHELL that targets Omron PLCs, and CODECALL that targets Schneider Electric PLCs are designed to be executed via a Command Line Interface.  Finally, LAZYCARGO (CVE-2020-15368) requires a command line to exploit the ASRock driver vulnerability on a Windows host. 
IT Cybersecurity and OT Cybersecurity personnel may be able to observe anomalous instances of command prompts in their environment. 
A total of 34 observables were identified with the use of the Command-Line Interface technique (T0807). This technique is important for investigation because it indicates the adversary is actively attempting to manually execute a malicious payload in the victim’s environment. This technique appears throughout the timeline and responding to it may halt further adversary activity within the victim’s environment, as well as prevent execution of malware that may result in disruption or destruction. Terminating the chain of techniques at this point may mitigate both further malicious activity within a victim’s environment and limit operational damage. 
Of the 34 observables associated with this technique, five are assessed to be highly perceivable.

The CODECALL module within the INCONTROLLER framework is capable of the Data Destruction technique. CODECALL can not only execute files on Schneider, CODESYS, and Modbus-enabled devices, but can delete files, as well. 
OT Staff and OT Cybersecurity personnel may be able to observe anomalous network traffic related to file deletion, as well as critical files missing from affected devices. 
A total of 17 observables were identified with the use of the Data Destruction technique (T0809). This technique is important for investigation because an adversary is attempting to inhibit properly functioning equipment within the OT environment and responding to it may prevent further disruption or damage. Terminating the chain of techniques at this point may potentially limit operational disruption or physical damage. 
Of the 17 observables associated with this technique, none are assessed to be highly perceivable.

The TAGRUN module within the INCONTROLLER framework is capable of the Monitor Process State technique (T0801). TAGRUN can query the state of OPC clients and servers within the OT environment over 4840 via read requests and read responses. The adversary would then likely export this data to a file that would be sent off to a C2 server to facilitate payload development and testing. OMSHELL is also capable of monitoring process states of Omron devices using a shell over Telnet and Omron’s proprietary FINS protocol.  
OT Staff and OT Cybersecurity personnel likely would not be able to observe anomalous OPC UA traffic over Port 4840. However, the prior anomalous ICMP Ping requests may also act as a triggering event before the Read Requests and Read Responses. 
A total of 22 observables were identified with the use of the Monitor Process State technique (T0801). This technique is important for investigation because an adversary is attempting to collect operational information on the victim’s OT environment. This technique appears throughout the timeline and responding to it may limit the methods of reconnaissance an adversary may undertake. Terminating the chain of techniques at this point may prevent the adversary from exfiltrating operational information. 
Of the 22 observables associated with this technique, six are assessed to be highly perceivable.

Several modules within INCONTROLLER leverage the Default Credentials technique (T0812) to facilitate lateral movement. OMSHELL and CODECALL can leverage hardcoded default credentials that Omron and Schneider Electric Devices come with from the factory. CODECALL may use CODESYS over UDP Port 1740 to brute force logins with default credentials or common passwords via a dictionary file.  Default credentials are often as simple as “password,” “admin,” or “root”. 
OT Staff and OT Cybersecurity personnel may be able to observe anomalous failed logins or brute forcing of Omron and Schneider Electric device interfaces. OT Staff and OT Cybersecurity may also observe anomalous failed login attempts against devices that use CODESYS due to CODECALL’s ability to interact with CODESYS-compatible devices. 
A total of 19 observables were identified with the use of the Default Credentials technique (T0812). This technique is important for investigation because adversaries can easily use hardcoded factory credentials that were not changed to gain further access into a victim’s OT environment.  This technique can appear throughout the timeline and responding to it may halt all future events. Terminating the chain of techniques at this point may halt an adversary’s options to conduct additional malicious activity in a victim’s environment. 
Of the 19 observables associated with this technique, three are assessed to be highly perceivable.

The CODECALL module within the INCONTROLLER framework is capable of the Denial of Control technique (T0813). CODECALL can sever CODESYS connections and disconnect active sessions with affected PLCs. CODECALL can crash logic on the controller, preventing any communications to the PLC unless the power is cycled.
OT Staff and OT Cybersecurity personnel may be able to observe unresponsive OT systems. 
A total of 11 observables were identified with the use of the Denial of Control technique (T0813). This technique is important for investigation because the adversary is actively conducting malicious activity within the OT environment and preventing authorized personnel and safety systems from preventing disruption or physical damage. This technique appears late in the timeline and responding to it is not likely to halt future events. Terminating the chain of techniques at this point is not likely to limit any operational disruption or physical damage.  
Of the 11 observables associated with this technique, three are assessed to be highly perceivable.

Numerous modules within the INCONTROLLER framework can conduct remote system discovery within a victim’s environment. ICECORE can use WMI for reconnaissance in the enterprise environment, likely identifying infrastructure suitable for pivoting into the OT environment or acting as a proxy node to external command and control infrastructure. TAGRUN uses OPC UA to identify all OPC UA configured clients and servers within a victim’s environment via an ICMP Ping sweep.  OMSHELL primarily uses FINS over User Datagram Protocol (UDP) to identify any Omron devices before conducting further probing via HTTP. CODECALL likely uses an initial batch of Address Resolution Protocol (ARP) calls to identify any networked devices and then use a UDP multicast over Port 27127 to identify any networked Schneider Electric devices. 
IT Staff, IT Cybersecurity, OT Staff, and OT Cybersecurity personnel may be able to observe anomalous network traffic related to WMI queries from ICECORE, anomalous OPC UA traffic, anomalous UDP broadcasts, or anomalous ARP calls in the OT environment. 
A total of 33 observables were identified with the use of the Remote System Discovery technique (T0846). This technique is important for investigation because this technique indicates an adversary is actively reconnoitering, and responding to it will prevent an adversary from gaining insight into the architecture of a victim’s OT environment. This technique appears in the middle of the timeline and responding to it will limit the adversary’s ability to detect and pivot to additional hosts within the victim’s operating environment. Terminating the chain of techniques at this point would limit the scope that an adversary can gain about an environment. 
Of the 33 observables associated with this technique, none are assessed to be highly perceivable.

Adversaries employing the INCONTROLLER framework may use the LAZYCARGO module’s Rootkit capability to bolster evasion. The adversary can install the signed AsrDrv103.sys driver that can act as a rootkit in a victim’s IT or OT environment.  This driver is vulnerable to CVE-2020-15368, allowing an adversary to execute code within the Windows kernel after installation of the vulnerable driver.  Some ASRock motherboards may be used in certain OT assets such as HMIs and Engineering workstations, although this CVE may be used in both enterprise and operations environments. 
IT Cybersecurity and OT Cybersecurity personnel may be able to observe anomalous program installation of either the AsrDrv103.sys file or additional payloads. 
A total of four observables were identified with the use of the Rootkit technique (T0851). This technique is important for investigation as rootkits are one of the stealthiest methods an adversary can use to conduct malicious activity in a victim’s environment. Responding to it will likely limit the ways an adversary can evade defender detection. This technique appears in the middle of the timeline and responding to it will limit the adversary’s ability to run malware components and modules.  Terminating the chain of techniques at this point would limit an adversary’s options for persisting in a victim’s environment. 
Of the four observables associated with this technique, none are assessed to be highly perceivable.

Adversaries using the INCONTROLLER framework may use the Change Operating mode technique for execution. OMSHELL can change operating modes of Omron PLCs for execution, and an adversary can manipulate exposed HTTP endpoints of Omron PLCs to change the operating mode of one or multiple targeted PLCs from “Program” to “Run.” 
OT Staff and OT Cybersecurity personnel may be able to observe anomalous HTTP traffic related to Omron’s proprietary FINS protocol. Additionally, OT Staff and OT Cybersecurity may also be able to observe anomalous operating mode changes on Omron PLCs. 
A total of 10 observables were identified with the use of the Change Operating Mode technique (T0890). This technique is important for investigation because it demonstrates the adversary has lower-level access to crucial systems and assets in the OT environment. This technique may appear throughout the timeline and responding to it will prevent adversary privilege escalation.  Terminating the chain of techniques at this point may halt some future events. 
Of the 10 observables associated with this technique, one is assessed to be highly perceivable.

Adversaries deploying the INCONTROLLER malware framework can employ the Change Operating Mode technique. OMSHELL can change the operation mode on Omron controllers, including the Monitor, Run, and Program modes.  
OT Staff and OT Cybersecurity personnel may be able to observe anomalous network traffic related to an adversary changing the operation mode of targeted PLCs, as well as anomalous system behavior on targeted Omron PLCs. 
A total of 37 observables were identified with the use of the Change Operating Mode technique (T0858). This technique is important for investigation because an adversary may change operating modes to cover up any prior malicious activities such as reconnaissance, and responding to it may limit an adversary’s reach in a targeted OT environment. This technique appears in the middle of the attack timeline, and responding to it will disrupt the adversary’s intrusion progression. Terminating the chain of techniques at this point may halt future adversary activity. 
Of the 37 observables associated with this technique, none are assessed to be highly perceivable.

Numerous modules within the INCONTROLLER framework can use the Valid Accounts technique to bolster persistence within a victim’s environment. Both OMSHELL and CODECALL are capable of using harvested credentials to interact with OT assets such as Engineering Workstations or HMIs. 
OT Cybersecurity personnel may be able to observe anomalous logins at unusual hours from either the enterprise environment or external adversary command and control infrastructure. 
A total of 18 observables were identified with the use of the Valid Accounts technique (T0859). This technique is important for investigation because malicious use of valid accounts is a stealthy way for an adversary to maintain persistence in a victim’s environment. This technique may appear throughout the timeline, and responding to it may limit an adversary’s access to the OT environment and OT assets. Terminating the chain of techniques at this point would limit the access and actions an adversary can take in the OT environment. 
Of the 18 observables associated with this technique, two are assessed to be highly perceivable.

Numerous modules within the INCONTROLLER framework can use the Valid Accounts technique (T0859) for lateral movement. The TAGRUN module can brute force logins into OPC UA servers using a hardcoded list of common passwords.   CODECALL can also brute force logins to Schneider PLCs over UDP Port 1740.  
OT Staff and OT Cybersecurity personnel may be able to observe logons with valid accounts at anomalous hours, as well as repeated failed logons. Observers may also be able to detect anomalous UDP traffic over Port 1740. 
A total of 17 observables were identified with the use of the Valid Accounts technique (T0859). This technique is important for investigation because an adversary will often use default or valid credentials to facilitate lateral movement into higher-privileged areas in the network. This technique can appear throughout the timeline and responding to it may halt further activity. Terminating the chain of techniques at this point would limit an adversary’s capability to move laterally throughout the victim’s OT environment. 
Of the 17 observables associated with this technique, five are assessed to be highly perceivable.

An adversary employing the INCONTROLLER framework would use the Scripting technique (T0853) to employ various tools within the framework. TAGRUN (MOUSEHOLE) uses an OPC UA Python library to help identify OPC UA clients and servers in a victim environment, which then is compiled into a logfile and exfiltrated to an adversary-controlled C2 server.  Additionally, Dragos states that TAGRUN, OMSHELL, CODECALL were written in Python as well. 
IT Cybersecurity, OT Staff, and OT Cybersecurity personnel may be able to observe anomalous Python scripts in their environment. However, since Python scripts may be obfuscated using randomized extensions and filenames, identification may not be readily apparent, although due to the many places an adversary can hide these files until needed for execution, it is unlikely that these anomalous python scripts would be observed
A total of 14 observables were identified with the use of the Scripting technique (T0853). This technique is important for investigation because the INCONTROLLER framework is largely Python-based and designed to be executed via the command line. This technique appears throughout the timeline, and responding to it will likely halt adversary activity in the OT environment. Terminating the chain of techniques at this point may halt future events. 
Of the 14 observables associated with this technique, five are assessed to be highly perceivable.

Two modules within the INCONTROLLER framework can use the Unauthorized Command Message technique (T0855). TAGRUN can not only read OPC UA values, but also write them. However, CyOTE analysts assess that TAGRUN is tool for reconnaissance and is unlikely to be used in the final stage of an OT cyber attack. The CODECALL module can send Modbus and CODESYS packets to Schneider Electric devices, as well as other brands of devices that can accept Modbus traffic. 
OT Staff and OT Cybersecurity personnel would likely not be able to observe malicious OPC UA values being written to devices or malicious Modbus and CODESYS packets in time to prevent operational disruption. 
A total of 15 observables were identified with the use of the Unauthorized Command Message technique (T0855). This technique is important for investigation because an adversary is attempting to manipulate OT assets. This technique appears late in the timeline and responding to it is unlikely to halt future events. Terminating the chain of techniques at this point in the timeline is unlikely to prevent disruption or destruction. 
Of the 15 observables associated with this technique, one is assessed to be highly perceivable.

An adversary deploying the INCONTROLLER framework may use the Native API technique (T0834) to facilitate malicious activity in a victim’s environment by leveraging native Windows tools. ICECORE leverages WMI to facilitate discovery, execution, and evasion from defenders. WMI is a native Windows tool that adversaries often use for reconnaissance, remote code execution, lateral movement, and persistence without the need to write any files to the disk. For remote access, WMI relies on Server Message Block (SMB) and Remote Procedure Call Service (RPCS) over Port 135 for remote access, presenting a potential observable opportunity for defenders. 
IT Staff and IT Cybersecurity personnel may be able to observe adversary activity in WMI Event Viewer, but this would be difficult to distinguish between normal observable events due to how often WMI is used for legitimate activity on the Windows OS. 
A total of three observables were identified with the use of the Native API technique (T0834). This technique is important for investigation, because in this instance WMI is a very effective tool for an adversary due to the breadth of its capability. This technique appears early in the timeline and responding to it will delay or deny adversary reconnaissance, privilege escalation, and pivoting into the OT environment. Terminating the chain of techniques at this point would likely halt further adversary activity such as reconnaissance in a victim’s IT environment. 
Of the three observables associated with this technique, none are assessed to be highly perceivable.

Several modules within the INCONTROLLER framework are capable of the Manipulation of Control technique (T0831). TAGRUN can write values to OPC clients and servers, allowing an adversary to manipulate any OT assets that are reliant on OPC UA. CODECALL is also able to manipulate Schneider Electric devices, as well as those that use Modbus and CODESYS. Finally, OMSHELL can manipulate both Omron PLCs as well as some Omron servo drives. 
OT Staff and OT Cybersecurity may be able to observe anomalous behavior from OPC, Omron, and Schneider Electric devices, as well as devices that use CODESYS and Modbus. 
A total of 22 observables were identified with the use of the Manipulation of Control technique (T0828). This technique is important for investigation because an adversary is actively manipulating OT assets to cause either operational disruption or physical damage, and responding to it is not likely to prevent damage or disruption. This technique appears at the end of the attack, and responding to it may prevent adversary’s from maliciously impacting some OT components. Terminating the chain of techniques at this point would not have a major effect. 
Of the 22 observables associated with this technique, 10 are assessed to be highly perceivable.

The OMSHELL module in the INCONTROLLER framework is capable of the Program Download technique (T0843). OMSHELL can load an attacker-customized configuration file to conduct malicious activity on infected Omron devices. CODECALL is also able to download adversary-customized files over CODESYS to a targeted PLC. 
OT Staff and OT Cybersecurity personnel may be able to observe anomalous network traffic associated with downloading an external program. OT Staff and OT Cybersecurity personnel may also observe anomalous files on Schneider Electric and Omron devices, or engineering workstations. 
A total of 23 observables were identified with the use of the Program Download technique (T0843). This technique is important for investigation as the adversary can load malicious software that can be used to cause a disruptive or destructive effect on OT assets.  Responding to it may halt all future events for Omron and Schneider devices, as well as those that use the Modbus or CODESYS protocols. This technique appears in the middle of the timeline and responding to it will limit the adversaries’ ability to move laterally within the system. Terminating the chain of techniques at this point would limit any operational damage or loss of productivity or revenue. 
Of the 23 observables associated with this technique, none are assessed to be highly perceivable.

OMSHELL is cable of the Program Upload technique to support collection in a victim’s OT environment.  An adversary employing OMSHELL would be able to harvest Omron PLC configuration files and load customized adversary-crafted configuration files. CODECALL may also be able to upload information deemed critical by an adversary via CODESYS or Modbus. 
OT Cybersecurity personnel may be able to observe anomalous configuration files on engineering workstations or the anomalous network traffic associated with file uploads. 
A total of 35 observables were identified with the use of the Program Upload technique (T0845). This technique is important for investigation because an adversary is attempting to gain crucial information on OT assets within a targeted environment, and responding to it may halt an adversary’s reconnaissance activities. This technique appears in the middle of the timeline and responding to it may limit the ability of adversaries to maliciously manipulate OT components. Terminating the chain of techniques at this point may halt some future events.  
Of the 35 observables associated with this technique, one is assessed to be highly perceivable.

Two modules within INCONTROLLER are capable of the Modify Parameter technique. CODECALL can read and write custom commands over Modbus to affected devices, as well as devices that rely on CODESYS to modify device parameters. ,  OMSHELL can modify the parameters of affected Omron devices that control physical processes such as motor speed or functions that detect overspeed conditions. 
OT Staff and OT Cybersecurity personnel may be able to observe anomalous behavior from Omron devices, as well as those that use Modbus and CODESYS. 
A total of 20 observables were identified with the use of the Modify Parameter technique (T0836). This technique is important for investigation because an adversary is actively tampering with parameters crucial for maintaining process integrity within the OT environment.  This technique appears late in the timeline and responding to it may prevent further disruption within the OT environment. Terminating the chain of techniques at this point may limit operational disruption or damage.  
Of the 20 observables associated with this technique, two are assessed to be highly perceivable.

The OMSHELL module within the INCONTROLLER framework is capable of the Network Sniffing technique (T0842). CISA notes that OMSHELL can parse HTTP response headers from Omron devices, allowing an adversary to glean detailed information about Omron assets in the victim’s environment.  OMSHELL is also able to perform general network traffic captures as well as retrieve the MAC addresses of Omron devices. 
OT Staff and OT Cybersecurity personnel may be able to observe anomalous files on infected hosts. Although INCONTROLLER was mostly composed of Python scripts when it was discovered, this could change in a real-world deployment.

Terminating the chain of techniques at this point may halt further adversary activity.
